lesson.title: The Energy Accounting of Chemistry: An Introduction to Thermodynamics
lesson.summary: Thermodynamics is the study of energy, especially heat, and how it flows and transforms during physical and chemical processes, all governed by the unbreakable rule that energy is conserved.
lesson.body:
Thermodynamics is the branch of chemistry concerned with energy: where it comes from, where it goes, and what form it takes during chemical reactions and physical changes. It answers questions such as why some reactions release noticeable warmth while others feel cold to the touch, why some reactions happen on their own while others require a continuous input of energy to proceed at all, and how much usable energy a given fuel can actually supply.

The foundation of thermodynamics is the law of conservation of energy, often called the first law of thermodynamics in this context: energy is never created or destroyed during an ordinary chemical or physical process, only transferred from one place to another or converted from one form into another. Because of this, whenever a reaction releases energy, that energy has to go somewhere specific, and whenever a reaction absorbs energy, that energy has to come from somewhere specific. Thermodynamics is, at its core, careful bookkeeping to track exactly where that energy travels.

Chemical reactions involve converting between different forms of energy. Reactant molecules hold chemical potential energy stored in their bonds. When those bonds break and new ones form, some of that potential energy can be converted into thermal energy, the kinetic energy of moving and vibrating particles, which is released to the surroundings as heat, or additional thermal energy can be drawn in from the surroundings to help break the original bonds in the first place.

To actually apply this kind of energy accounting to a real reaction, chemists first need a precise way to describe exactly what is being tracked, called the system, versus everything else, called the surroundings, along with a way to classify how freely a given system trades matter and energy with those surroundings. They also need language to describe whether a specific reaction releases energy to its surroundings or draws energy in from them, and a clear distinction between the total energy transferred during a process and how hot or cold something actually feels. Those are exactly the ideas the chapters that follow work through one at a time.
